name: Herodias
source_summary: Wife first of Herod Philip and then, unlawfully, of his brother Herod Antipas; she resented John the Baptist for condemning the marriage and used her daughter's dance at a banquet to manipulate Herod into having John beheaded.
family_friendly_summary: Herodias was married to Herod Philip, but she left him to marry his brother, Herod Antipas, instead -- a marriage John the Baptist publicly condemned as against God's law. Herodias resented John deeply for this and wanted him killed, but Herod protected John because he respected him. At a birthday banquet, Herodias's daughter danced so well that Herod promised her anything she wanted. Herodias saw her chance and told her daughter to ask for John the Baptist's head on a platter. Herod reluctantly agreed, and John was executed. Herodias's story is a sobering example of using someone else, even one's own daughter, to carry out a plan for revenge.
adult_story: Herodias, granddaughter of Herod the Great, was first married to Herod Philip (referred to in the Gospels simply as Philip), but left him to marry his brother Herod Antipas instead, a union John the Baptist publicly denounced as unlawful, since Philip was still living: 'It is not lawful for you to have her' (Mark 6:17-18). Herodias resented John bitterly for this and 'wanted to put him to death,' but could not, because Herod himself protected John, respecting him as a righteous and holy man even while keeping him imprisoned (6:19-20). Her opportunity came at Herod's birthday banquet, when her daughter danced before Herod and his guests and pleased him so much that he swore an oath to give her whatever she asked, up to half his kingdom (6:21-23). The girl went out and asked her mother what to request, and Herodias answered immediately and specifically: 'the head of John the Baptist' (6:24). Her daughter returned at once and demanded it be brought on a platter, and Herod, though grieved, honored his rash oath rather than be shamed before his guests, sending an executioner to behead John in prison (6:25-27). Herodias's calculated use of the banquet's public pressure and her own daughter's request to accomplish what Herod's own conscience had been resisting stands as Scripture's clearest picture of manipulation aimed squarely at securing personal revenge.
christ_connections: Herodias's determination to silence John the Baptist -- the very voice calling Israel to repentance -- previews the world's broader resistance to the gospel's call to turn from sin, a resistance that ultimately falls on the One John himself pointed toward (John 1:29).
devotionals: Herodias’s story teaches us about manipulation for revenge; may we look to Jesus, whose grace and truth never fail.
Through Herodias’s experience of complicity in murder, God teaches us to trust His wisdom and follow Jesus faithfully.
